newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE - Canadian energy producers gird for battle.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Canadian energy producers gird for battle.

text.p: A fierce battle mixing energy, chemicals and politics threatens to cast a giant shadow over the natural gas pipeline that snakes through the oil-rich Canadian province of Alberta.

The fight is shaping up over whether to pump ethane -- a liquid biproduct of natural gas -- south to the United States for processing by chemical companies, or whether it should be processed at expensive new plants set up inside Canada.

The battle is pitting Alberta's powerful oil and gas producers against a burgeoning petrochemical industry, with politicians vacillating in the middle and all sides struggling to quantify how much the ethane may be worth.

Alberta's Conservative government, long known as a staunch defender of free enterprise, is also interested in sheltering its own industries. It therefore risks being caught in the crossfire and becoming the main casualty in the clash.

Ethane, a light hydrocarbon that often flows out of wells with natural gas, is used by chemical companies to make ethylene -- a feedstock for polyethylene. Polyethylene, in turn, is used to produce common consumer packaging and such ubiquitous items as plastic shopping bags.
NOVA Corp, the Canadian pipeline and petrochemical concern, and the Canadian unit of the giant Dow Chemical Corp operate major ethylene plants in Alberta.
Ethane can also be left in natural gas pipelines and burned with the rest of the heating fuel -- an alternative that strips it of most of its value.

NOVA has a 12-billion-cubic-feet-per-day monopoly on gas transport in Alberta. It has already announced plans with Union Carbide Corp this year for a US$600-million expansion to the two companies' huge ethylene processing complex at Joffre in central Alberta.

NOVA and Union Carbide say a key factor in their decision to build the expansion, called E-III, was Alberta's growing supply of ethane, bought at times for a quarter of the U.S. Gulf Coast region spot price.

NOVA has enjoyed low feedstock costs as a result of 20-year contracts for ethane in which prices are tied to those in natural gas markets. The first contract ends in 1998, the second in 2004. In the second quarter of this year, when the Gulf Coast ethane price was 26 U.S. cents per gallon, NOVA was touting Alberta supply costs of seven cents a gallon.

Such comments did not go unnoticed by already disgruntled producers, especially a group of 17 aiming to build a C$3.4 billion gas liquids-rich pipeline gas line to Chicago from northeast British Columbia by 2000.

Companies backing the proposed Alliance Pipeline project, which include producers like Gulf Canada Resources Ltd, Crestar Energy Inc and Petro-Canada and pipeline heavyweight IPL Energy Inc, plan to ship the liquids out of Alberta to feed their own ethane extraction facilities planned south of the border near Chicago.
The pipeline would transport ethane produced in the gas fields of northeast British Columbia. More could be injected into the line at Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, a petrochemical hub outside Edmonton.
Alliance vice-president Jack Crawford maintains liquids transport is not critical to the project but would allow the group to offer more as a new player in the industry.
"We would anticipate that producers would earn a higher netback on the ethane component of their stream by using our system," he said.

But analysts contend the liquids portion of Alliance's plans is crucial to developing the pipeline, which would pump at much higher pressure than straight natural gas lines. Without the value added by transporting ethane, Alliance's tolls for transporting gas would be much higher than the existing pipeline systems, said Sam Kanes, analyst with ScotiaMcleod Inc "It wouldn't work," Kanes said, especially if Alliance and the 1998 expansion of the Saskatchewan-to-Chicago Northern Border gas pipeline go ahead and flood the Chicago market with new supply, lowering prices there.
NOVA has already sounded a warning that petrochemical jobs and economic benefits would flow out of Alberta to the United States along with the ethane in the Alliance pipeline.

"Further expansion of an Alberta-based chemicals industry requires that natural gas liquids be extracted from the gas stream before the gas leaves Canada," NOVA's chief executive Ted Newall cautioned at the company's annual meeting in April. "Alberta's loss would be America's gain."
NOVA reckons producers would also get much less than than the current value if Alberta ethane prices were set on a Gulf Coast-minus-transport basis in a competitive market.

"I would say that you end up with higher value by converting it (to polyethylene) in Alberta," said NOVA Chemicals vice- president Bud Clark, citing studies over the past decade that have shown the cost of transporting ethane to the U.S. erased any benefit of higher prices for producers.
One thing both sides agree on is that Alberta's provincial government is heading for a delicate balancing act as the battle over ethane heats up.

Alberta's premier Ralph Klein's administration is actively trying to attract more chemical and manufacturing projects to the province by cutting industrial taxes and promoting a business-friendly economic environment.
But it has also worked hard to deregulate its energy industry and allow producers to control their own destinies.
"It's a sticky point," conceded a source within the Alberta energy department. "There are certain conflicting objectives there as to what your optimal value-added is."
Meanwhile, Alberta's politicians are reluctant to choose sides, hoping the agument will be settled by the industry. That seems unlikely.
Crawford believes NOVA's plans would not be stymied by higher supply costs. If anything, the plant's payback would only be take longer, he said.
"Perhaps, if anything, you're trading off some profit that NOVA might make for some profit that some producers might make," he said.
Whatever the outcome of the conflict, observers claim it is likely to mean higher ethane prices for Canadian producers.
Either NOVA will be forced to pay more for its supply, "or the product will leave the province if there's enough pipe to look for the best netback," said ScotiaMcleod's Kane.
